title: Union Health Ministry Reviews Progress Towards Achieving Malaria Elimination Target by 2030
subtitle:
​​​​​​​Focused, area-specific strategies and strengthened surveillance are essential to accelerate India’s progress towards malaria elimination by 2030: Smt. Aradhana Patnaik, Additional Secretary and Mission Director, National Health Mission (NHM)
India records nearly 80% decline in malaria cases and deaths between 2015 and 2025; number of high-burden districts declines from 155 to 33
160 districts reported zero indigenous malaria cases during 2022–2025
body_text:
Emphasising India’s commitment to achieving the Sustainable Development Goal of malaria elimination by 2030, Smt. Aradhana Patnaik, Additional Secretary and Mission Director, National Health Mission (NHM), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, chaired a high-level review meeting with senior officers of the Ministry, National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC), Mission Directors of National Health Missions and District Collectors of concerned States and districts.
India has made significant progress in reducing the burden of malaria through sustained and focused public health interventions. Between 2015 and 2025, malaria cases and deaths in the country declined by nearly 80% , while the number of high-burden districts decreased from 155 to 33 . As many as 160 districts reported zero indigenous malaria cases during 2022–2025 , reflecting sustained interruption of local transmission and the success of focused malaria control and elimination interventions.
The review focused on the 33 high-burden districts across nine States and Union Territories, which accounted for 64% of malaria cases and 54% of malaria deaths reported in 2025 . Detailed State-wise reviews were undertaken for Mizoram, Odisha, Tripura, Assam, Andhra Pradesh, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Maharashtra.
Smt. Aradhana Patnaik emphasised the need to maintain a high level of vigilance and adopt focused, area-specific strategies to effectively prevent and eliminate malaria. She stressed the importance of effective implementation of District Action Plans in all 33 high-burden districts, along with Village Action Plans in high-burden villages, to ensure targeted interventions based on local epidemiological and geographical conditions.
Highlighting the importance of early detection and complete treatment, the meeting stressed the need to strengthen the Test, Treat and Track strategy. Delays in diagnosis and treatment were identified as critical factors contributing to malaria deaths. States were advised to strengthen active surveillance and ensure uninterrupted availability of diagnostics and anti-malarial drugs, particularly in hard-to-reach and vulnerable areas.
The review also underscored the need to further strengthen surveillance systems and improve data quality. States were advised to review unusually high Annual Blood Examination Rates (ABER) to identify possible duplicate testing, repeated entries and inclusion of asymptomatic screening. It was emphasised that asymptomatic cases detected through mass screening should be reported separately and excluded from API and ABER calculations to ensure accurate assessment of the malaria situation and programme performance.
Smt. Aradhana Patnaik further stressed the importance of intersectoral convergence for achieving malaria elimination. She noted that health interventions alone cannot address several factors contributing to malaria transmission, including water-logging, source reduction and environmental management. States were therefore advised to strengthen coordination with the Departments of Rural Development and Urban Development, as well as Panchayati Raj Institutions, for effective implementation of environmental and vector-control measures.
Greater engagement of Self-Help Groups, community volunteers and Panchayati Raj representatives was also encouraged to strengthen community participation in early reporting of fever cases, identification of water-logging and other mosquito breeding sites, and implementation of source-reduction activities.
The meeting was attended by Shri Prabhakar, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; Shri Nikhil Gajraj, Joint Secretary (VBD), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; Dr. Tanu Jain, Director, NCVBDC; Mission Directors of NHM; State Programme Officers of the concerned States; District Collectors; Chief Medical Officers and District Malaria Officers of the concerned districts.

ministry.name: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

enrichment.summary: The Union Health Ministry, through NHM Mission Director Aradhana Patnaik, reviewed India's progress toward the SDG target of malaria elimination by 2030. Between 2015 and 2025, malaria cases and deaths fell by nearly 80%, high-burden districts dropped from 155 to 33, and 160 districts reported zero indigenous cases during 2022-2025. The review focused on the remaining 33 high-burden districts across nine states/UTs, which accounted for 64% of cases and 54% of deaths in 2025, and stressed strengthening surveillance, the Test-Treat-Track strategy, and intersectoral convergence.
enrichment.context:
India's malaria elimination effort is guided by the National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016-2030) and the National Strategic Plan for Malaria Elimination, aligned with the WHO's Global Technical Strategy for Malaria and India's commitment under SDG 3 to end epidemics of malaria by 2030. India was recognised by the WHO for being removed from the 'high burden to high impact' list of countries in recent years, reflecting sustained decline in case burden. Key programmatic tools include Annual Parasite Incidence (API) and Annual Blood Examination Rate (ABER) as surveillance metrics, District and Village Action Plans for localized interventions, and the Test-Treat-Track strategy for early case management.

The review's emphasis on intersectoral convergence — linking health interventions with rural/urban development departments and Panchayati Raj Institutions for water-logging control and vector-breeding site management — reflects a broader public health lesson that vector-borne disease control cannot be achieved through curative health services alone but requires environmental management, community participation, and administrative coordination across sectors. This mirrors similar convergence approaches used in India's fight against other vector-borne diseases like dengue, lymphatic filariasis, and kala-azar.

prelims_questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding India's progress on malaria elimination as reviewed by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare:
1. Malaria cases and deaths in India declined by nearly 80% between 2015 and 2025.
2. The number of high-burden malaria districts in India decreased from 155 to 33 during this period.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
prelims_questions.explanation: As per the release, both statements are correct: malaria cases/deaths declined nearly 80% between 2015-2025, and high-burden districts fell from 155 to 33 in the same period.

prelims_questions.question: In the context of India's malaria surveillance programme, what does 'Annual Blood Examination Rate (ABER)' refer to?
options: The rate of malaria deaths per 100,000 population annually
The percentage of population screened for malaria through blood examination in a year relative to total population
The annual rate of anti-malarial drug resistance detected in blood samples
The ratio of confirmed to suspected malaria cases in a district
prelims_questions.explanation: ABER is a key malaria surveillance indicator representing the proportion of population blood-tested for malaria in a given year; the release notes concerns about unusually high ABER due to duplicate testing or asymptomatic screening inflating figures.

mains_questions.question: India aims to eliminate malaria by 2030 in line with SDG targets. Discuss the strategies adopted by India for malaria elimination and the challenges that remain in high-burden districts.
Vector-borne disease control requires intersectoral convergence beyond the health sector. Examine this statement with reference to India's malaria elimination programme.

study_notes.reason: The release carries testable factual data (targets, statistics, surveillance metrics, strategy names) and also substantive analytical material on why India's vector-borne disease control needs intersectoral convergence beyond curative health measures.

prelims.point: India's malaria elimination target aligned with SDG 3 is 2030, guided by the National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016-2030)
prelims.why_important: Target year and framework name are classic objective-question material for health-related SDG commitments.

prelims.point: Test-Treat-Track is the core strategy for malaria case management in India
prelims.why_important: A named strategy that could be tested for its definition or matched with the disease it targets.

prelims.point: Annual Parasite Incidence (API) and Annual Blood Examination Rate (ABER) are key malaria surveillance metrics
prelims.why_important: UPSC frequently tests definitions and distinctions between similar-sounding technical indices used in disease surveillance.

prelims.point: Between 2015-2025, malaria cases and deaths in India declined by nearly 80%, and high-burden districts fell from 155 to 33
prelims.why_important: A specific statistic that could appear in a factual statement-based question on malaria progress.

prelims.point: NCVBDC (National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control) functions under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare as the nodal body for vector-borne disease control
prelims.why_important: Institutional identity and parent ministry linkage is a standard prelims testable fact.

prelims.point: India was removed from WHO's 'high burden to high impact' list of malaria-affected countries
prelims.why_important: A specific WHO classification status change that could be used as a factual marker of India's progress.

mains.point: Malaria elimination requires intersectoral convergence beyond curative health services, involving rural/urban development departments and Panchayati Raj Institutions for environmental and vector-control management
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on why disease elimination programmes require multi-departmental coordination rather than health-sector action alone, applicable to vector-borne diseases broadly.

mains.point: Data quality issues in surveillance, such as inflated ABER from duplicate testing and asymptomatic mass screening, can distort the accurate picture of disease burden
mains.analytical_use: Relevant for questions on challenges in health programme monitoring and evaluation, and the need for robust data systems in evidence-based policymaking.

mains.point: Delays in diagnosis and treatment remain a critical factor contributing to residual malaria deaths despite overall decline
mains.analytical_use: Supports answers on persistent implementation gaps in disease elimination even after significant aggregate progress, especially in hard-to-reach areas.

mains.point: Community participation through Self-Help Groups, volunteers and Panchayati Raj representatives is being leveraged for early reporting and source reduction
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on the role of grassroots institutions and community participation in achieving public health goals.
